Submarine relief Continental Rise Abyssal Plain Mid-Ocean Ridge Rift Valley Magma Trench Continent Continental Shelf Continental Slope Abyssal Hill Seamount Submarine Canyon Volcanic Island Oceans cover most of our planet and conceal many secrets beneath their waters. Have you ever wondered what the land under the oceans looks like, why ocean water is always moving, or what wealth and resources lie beneath the sea? How do areas like maritime zones help countries use the oceans, and how can we protect ourselves from ocean hazards, such as cyclones and tsunamis?

In this chapter, we will explore these human–ocean connections and discover how oceans shape both our daily lives and the world around us. Ocean Relief As we explore human–ocean connections, let us begin with the ocean floor and its features. Just as land has mountains, valleys, and plains, the ocean floor, too, has several landforms, together known as submarine relief or ocean relief. These include underwater mountains, valleys, plateaus, and trenches. The Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean is the deepest place on Earth, while the Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world's longest mountain range, hidden beneath the ocean.
Some underwater mountains like Mauna Kea (Hawai'i) are even taller than Mount Everest.

1 – Oceans and Life Important submarine relief features Seamounts are often volcanic, with some flattened by wave action over millennia to form guyots. Seamounts and Guyots The deepest parts of the ocean. Ocean Trenches An immense underwater mountain range formed by volcanic activity. Mid-Ocean Ridge The vast, flat, and deep ocean floor. Abyssal Plain The submerged, shallow edge of a continent; extends under the ocean. Rich in marine life and resources like oil and gas. Continental Shelf The steep slope marking the true edge of a continent.

Guyot: A flat-topped underwater mountain, usually a former seamount whose summit was eroded and later submerged.

Understanding Society: India and Beyond Grade 9 Part 2 Movement of Ocean Water—Waves, Tides, and Currents The water in the oceans is constantly in motion. Waves, tides, and currents are not merely movements of ocean water; they help shape the Earth's surface, support marine life, aid fishing and travel, and even influence climate. Let us learn more about these oceanic movements. Waves When the surface of the ocean rises and falls alternately, it is called a wave. Waves are primarily caused by winds blowing across the water. They carry energy across the oceans over long distances.

Observe Fig. 1.3 and note the crests (high peaks) and troughs (lower valleys). Waves are often called coastal architects as they shape the shoreline through erosion and sediment transport. Observe the various landforms formed by waves in Fig. 1.4 and note how wave action creates erosional features, such as sea cracks, caves, arches, sea stacks, and stumps. Also notice the original headland shown in the figure. In addition to erosional landforms, waves also form depositional features such as beaches.

During storms, strong winds can generate huge waves that may cause significant damage along coastlines. The giant waves majorly caused by underwater earthquakes are called tsunamis, which can be extremely destructive. On reaching the shore, tsunamis may attain a maximum vertical height above sea level, known as the run-up height, of up to 30 metres, or even more in extreme cases. Tides Tides are the rhythmic rise and fall of ocean water that occur twice a day in most parts of the world.

When the water rises to its highest level and covers much of the shore, it is called high tide (flood tide). When the water falls to its lowest level and moves away from the shore, it is called low tide (ebb tide). Observe Fig. 1.5 and note the change in water level during high and low tides. Do you notice the oval layer around the Earth indicating water level? Can you also see how the water level rises during high tide and falls during low tide? Hydraulic action: The erosion of rock and soil caused by the force of moving water, which loosens and removes material.

1 – Oceans and Life Sun and the Moon acts in different directions. As a result, the difference between high tide and low tide becomes smaller, producing neap tides. Fig. 1.6 shows the levels of high and low water during both spring and neap tides, along with the average low-water levels for each. High tides are important for navigation because they raise the water level near the shore, allowing ships to enter harbours more easily. In ports and coastal areas, tidal information is essential, as tidal ranges in some ports can reach 4–5 metres. The Gulf of Khambhat has one of the highest tidal ranges, at about 12 metres.

Before a ship berths at a port, it must check both the water depth and the tidal range to ensure safe docking, especially during low tide. Some sea channels, such as the Singapore Strait, contain shallow areas. Hence, ships such as Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) passing through these regions often wait for hours to transit only during high tide to ensure sufficient water depth and avoid running aground. Tidal changes also generate strong currents because large volumes of water flow in and out of coastal areas.

These tidal currents can reach speeds of 5–6 knots (about 9–11 km/h). Fig. 1.7. Observe how high and low tides help in fishing activities High tide Low tide High tides also support fishing activities (Fig. 1.7). During high tide, many fish move closer to the shore in search of food and shelter, enabling fishing communities to obtain a better catch. The rise and fall of tidal water are also used to generate electricity in some places (Fig. 1.8). India has a vast coastline of 11,098.81 kilometres, and although tidal energy is not yet widely used on a large scale, certain areas have been identified as suitable for its development.
The Gulf of Kutch, the Gulf of Khambhat, and the Sundarbans are among the major tidal energy sites in India.

Ocean Currents Ocean currents are continuous streams of water that flow across the ocean surface in definite directions (Fig. 1.9). They are caused by factors, such as winds, the Earth's rotation (Coriolis force), differences in temperature and salinity, and the shape of continents and ocean basins. Ocean currents may be warm or cold depending on the direction from which the water flows. Currents flowing from warmer regions are called warm currents, while those flowing from colder regions are called cold currents. On maps, warm currents are usually shown in red and cold currents in blue.

THINK ABOUT IT Observe the map carefully and note the movement patterns of cold and warm currents. Do you think these currents affect the temperature of nearby coastal regions? The Gulf Stream, a warm current originating in the Gulf of Mexico in the Atlantic Ocean, flows towards Norway and keeps its waters relatively warm. As a result, sea ice does not form easily in the Norwegian region despite its high latitude (60°–70°). In contrast, the Labrador Current, a cold current flowing along the east coast of Canada, carries freezing water and supports the formation of sea ice and icebergs even at lower latitudes.

Cyclones and Tsunamis—Early Warning Systems Oceans and seas can give rise to sudden natural hazards such as cyclones, which are large rotating storms, and tsunamis, which are giant waves caused by earthquakes. To protect people from such dangers, scientists have developed Early Warning Systems that work like giant alarm systems for coastal areas.

To reduce risks, people, communities, and governments must act in advance. Early Warning Systems help detect cyclones and tsunamis, predict disasters, and issue timely warnings so that people can evacuate and stay safe. Talk to your elders and find out whether similar folk traditions or stories related to natural disasters exist in your culture. Share these with your classmates and discuss how traditional knowledge can help communities stay safe. India has several Cyclone Warning Services and Marine Weather Services that monitor storms along both the eastern and western coasts. For early warning systems to be effective, they must function continuously.

India uses advanced technologies to predict cyclones at an early stage, which has significantly reduced the loss of human and animal lives. The Government of India has launched the National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project (NCRMP) to build cyclone shelters, strengthen warning systems, and improve emergency response mechanisms. The project focuses on cyclone-prone States and Union Territories and includes a Decision Support System (DSS) for disaster management authorities.

The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), in collaboration with the India Meteorological Department (IMD), has also established the Storm Surge Early Warning System (SSEWS) for the Indian coasts. Its main objective is to protect coastal communities by forecasting cyclone-induced storm surges and the extent of coastal inundation.

Understanding Society: India and Beyond Grade 9 Part 2 DON'T MISS OUT On 26 December 2004, the world witnessed unprecedented devastation caused by the Indian Ocean Tsunami. The disaster claimed around 2,30,000 lives and caused severe environmental damage across many countries bordering the Indian Ocean. India was among the worst-affected countries, as massive waves swept away people and structures along the coasts. Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, Andhra Pradesh, Keralam, and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands especially suffered extensive damage.

The scale of the disaster led many countries to establish effective tsunami early warning systems and stronger disaster-management mechanisms. Under an initiative of the Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC), the Government of India set up a real-time network of tsunami detection buoys (Fig. 1.14) designed to detect, measure, and monitor tsunamis. Understanding Society: India and Beyond Grade 9 Part 2 For an early warning system to save lives, information must reach the public quickly and effectively. The Indian Tsunami Early Warning Centre (ITEWC) is tasked with sending alerts to the Government of India, which then informs state governments and emergency response teams. Reliable communication is ensured through satellite-based communication networks, SMS, emails, and coastal display boards. Besides technology, public awareness and training programmes are equally important for an effective early warning system.

Educating officials and coastal communities on how to interpret warnings helps ensure that when disasters such as cyclones are predicted, people know how to respond appropriately. Marine Resources and Their Significance Do you recall learning about natural resources in the Grade 8 Social Science Part 1 textbook? These resources are obtained from land, water, forests and animals, and other natural sources.

Oceans, too, are vast storehouses of resources, and the materials and features found in oceans that have intrinsic or economic value are called marine resources. Marine resources can be broadly classified into two categories—Marine Living Resources and Marine Non-living Resources. They include fish and seafood, biodiversity, oil and natural gas, minerals, sand and gravel, renewable blue energy sources such as tidal and wave energy, tourism potential, and unique ecosystems such as coral reefs. Fig. 1.17 presents a detailed classification of marine resources.

Significance of Marine Resources Marine resources are vital for food security, economic activities, and maintaining a healthy environment (Fig. 1.17). Countries with long coastlines, such as India, benefit greatly from the sea. Fishing, trade, and tourism provide livelihoods to millions of people, while oceans also support biodiversity and sustain numerous plant and animal species. However, marine resources must be used responsibly without disturbing marine ecosystems.

Significance of marine resources Food and Livelihood: Fish are a major source of protein, while fishing and aquaculture support important industries and livelihoods. Energy: Offshore oil and gas reserves; immense potential for renewable 'blue energy' from tides and waves. Trade and Tourism: 90% of global trade by volume is carried by sea; coastal tourism is a multi-billion dollar industry.

Cultural Significance: The sacred śhaṅkha (conch) and kapardikā (cowrie shells), once used as currency, are regarded as divine treasures from the mythological Samudra Manthana, reflecting the close connection among the sea, prosperity, and culture. Minerals and Materials: Sand, gravel, and deep- sea minerals. The Ocean is a Vast Storehouse of Resources Vital for Life, Livelihoods, and Culture Marine resources hold immense value for humanity and for coastal nations like India, they are the bedrock of local economies and traditions.

The role of Blue Economy Maritime Zones Have you ever wondered who owns the oceans and how countries decide where they can fish or travel?

To understand this, we need to learn about maritime zones—different areas of the ocean defined by international law. The sea area closest to a country is called its territorial waters, over which the country has near-complete control, subject to the right of innocent passage for foreign ships. Just as on land, the government can make laws relating to customs, immigration, and pollution control in this zone. Observe Fig. 1.20 and note the extent of the territorial sea in nautical miles.

Beyond this lies the contiguous zone, extending from the baseline up to 24 nautical miles, where the country has limited control over customs, fiscal matters, and illegal immigration. Nautical mile: A unit of measurement used in maritime and air navigation. It is defined as exactly 1,852 metres (about 6,076 feet). Based on the Earth's circumference, one nautical mile corresponds to one minute of latitude making it a convenient unit for charting and navigation across the world's seas.

Maritime zones (Indicative only) DON'T MISS OUT Innocent Passage is a principle that allows foreign ships to pass through the territorial waters of a country as long as they do not threaten its peace, good order, or security. Ships must move continuously without stopping, except in emergencies or cases of breakdowns. This right does not permit activities such as fishing, military operations, or other non-peaceful actions.

Beyond the contiguous zone, lie the Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs), which extend from the baseline up to 200 nautical miles from the coast, and are defined under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) by global agreement. In these zones, a country has special rights to use ocean resources, such as fish, oil, and gas, although ships from other countries may still pass through peacefully. It is important to note, however, that the country does not fully own or control the waters of the EEZ. Beyond the EEZs of all countries lie the high seas, also known as international waters.

Covering about 64 per cent of the world's oceans, these waters do not belong to any single country and are therefore considered part of the global commons. All countries enjoy equal rights on the high seas, including navigation, fishing, flying over them, laying undersea cables, building lawful structures such as artificial lands, and exploring for minerals.

Understanding Society: India and Beyond Grade 9 Part 2 Although the high seas are essential, they also present many challenges. Since no single country controls them, issues, such as overfishing, illegal fishing, and conflicts over resources often arise. These problems affect millions of people who depend on the sea for food and livelihoods. Ensuring navigation and safety is also more difficult without clear enforcement mechanisms. On the high seas, the laws of the flag state—the country in which a ship is registered—apply.

International Maritime Rules and Regulations In the earlier sections of this chapter, you learnt that oceans are vital for trade, travel, and communication. To ensure that activities at sea remain safe, fair, and peaceful, countries follow a set of international rules and agreements known as maritime law or maritime regulations. These laws regulate how ships operate and move; protect the marine environment; address issues such as piracy, terrorism, natural disasters, and accidents; safeguard trade routes; and help settle disputes between countries.

LET'S EXPLORE Maritime disputes are conflicts or disagreements between countries over territory, resources, or rights in naval areas such as oceans, seas, or coastal regions. Can you find out some countries that have conflicts over their territorial sea waters? Important Maritime Rules and Regulations Just as there are traffic rules on land, ships must follow "rules of the road at sea" to avoid accidents.

These rules, known as COLREGs (Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea), include maintaining a proper lookout, deciding which side to pass on, identifying the give-way and stand-on vessels, proceeding at a safe speed, and using lights, sound signals, shapes (for different types of vessels such as fishing boats), along with appropriate actions to prevent collisions. In addition, ships use international signals and radio communication to share information and prevent accidents, especially in crowded or hazardous waters.

1 – Oceans and Life Ships must also meet safety standards and are prohibited from polluting the seas. The MARPOL (International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships) Convention is an important international agreement aimed at reducing pollution from ships. Why are Maritime Rules Important? International maritime rules, regulations, and agreements help keep the oceans safe and ensure the fair and sustainable use of ocean resources. These rules enable countries to cooperate in using marine resources without conflict while protecting marine life, ships, sailors, and coastal communities.

Without such regulations, the oceans could become dangerous and chaotic, with increased pollution, accidents, collisions, and disputes over resources. By establishing common standards for all ships, regardless of the country they belong to, maritime rules help keep the oceans safe, clean, and open for trade and travel.

Before we move on… Æ Oceans are vital for global trade, travel, communication, and climate regulation. Æ Movements of ocean water—waves, tides, and currents—affect marine ecosystems, global climate, and human activities like fishing and navigation. Æ Maritime zones include territorial waters, EEZs (Exclusive Economic Zones), and the high seas. Æ Sustainable use of marine resources through cooperation, regulation, and conservation is essential to protect aquatic life and support future generations. Æ Maritime rules and regulations exist to resolve disputes over marine boundaries. Life on Earth Chapter 2 1. How do physiography and climate shape life on Earth? 2. How are humans and other life forms interconnected? 3. What is the importance of preserving various life forms, and how can we contribute to their conservation? The Big Questions Geography helps us understand how climate, landforms, and water shape life on Earth—and how humans adapt their lives to these conditions. From forests and grasslands to deserts and coastal regions, different environments support different forms of life. At the same time, human activities influence these natural systems in significant ways.

This chapter explores the close relationships among physical features, climate, and living organisms, and encourages us to reflect on our responsibility towards preserving the diversity of life on Earth. Imagine our planet as a giant patchwork quilt, where each patch has its own colours, weather, and living beings. These huge patches are called biomes. The word 'biome' is made up of the word bio, derived from the Greek word bios, meaning 'life', and -ome, a suffix used in biology to denote a group of a specific type of biological constituents.

Biomes are large natural regions of the world where certain types of plants and animals live under similar climatic conditions. For example, icy tundras, hot deserts, green forests, and vast grasslands are all different types of biomes. In simple terms, a biome is like a broad environmental region, while an ecosystem is like a neighbourhood within it, where plants, animals, and non-living things interact closely. Each biome is unique, but together they form the living world of our planet, supporting diverse forms of life and helping maintain the balance of nature. Fig. 2.1. Earth as a giant patchwork quilt

Æ Why are there areas that do not have any specific biomes? Types of Biomes Now that you have understood the meaning and uniqueness of biomes, let us identify the different types of biomes.

Different biomes support diverse plant and animal life and can be categorised into terrestrial (land-based) and aquatic biomes (water-based). There are several factors that determine which types of plants and animals can survive and thrive in a biome. These include temperature, precipitation patterns, dominant plant species, growth forms of vegetation, etc.

2 – Life on Earth Terrestrial Biomes Terrestrial biomes are classified into forests, grasslands, deserts, and tundra, based on their climate. Forest Biome A forest biome is like nature's giant green umbrella—warm, wet, and bursting with life at every level, from the tallest trees to the damp forest floor. Tropical rainforests are mainly found near the Equator, between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° N to 23.5° S). These regions remain hot and wet throughout the year, which supports the growth of dense forests.

The largest tropical rainforests are located in the Amazon Basin in South America, the Congo Basin in Africa, and parts of Southeast Asia, such as Indonesia and Malaysia. Smaller rainforest regions are also found in Central America, as well as in India's Andaman & Nicobar Islands, and the Northeastern states. Together, these areas form the world's richest storehouse of biodiversity with rich genetic resources. They preserve unique genetic material, supporting conservation and scientific research, and are hence also known as a 'gene bank'. Forests also play an important role in maintaining oxygen levels and balancing the Earth's climate.

Interconnectedness between Biomes and Living Beings Biomes are closely connected to living beings because they provide a natural environment where plants, animals, and humans can survive and interact. At the same time, living beings also influence biomes—animals help in pollination and seed dispersal, humans modify landscapes for farming or cities, and microorganisms recycle nutrients. In this way, biomes and living beings are interconnected systems that depend on one another to maintain ecological balance and biodiversity. We will discuss some of the aspects of this interconnectedness in the following section.

Maintaining Ecological Balance and Biodiversity Biodiversity Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth, including plants, animals, microorganisms, and the ecosystems they inhabit (Fig. 2.11). It refers not only to the number of different species but also to the genetic differences within species and the variety of habitats and ecological processes that sustain life. In simple terms, biodiversity means the richness of life forms and the natural balance they create, which is essential for maintaining healthy ecosystems and supporting human survival. Fig. 2.11. Understanding Society: India and Beyond Grade 9 Part 2 The geographical aspects of biodiversity conservation focus on how location, climate, landforms, and ecosystems influence the protection and management of living organisms. Since biodiversity is unevenly distributed across the Earth, geography plays a vital role in conservation. Some key aspects of conservation are— Hotspots of Biodiversity: Certain regions, such as the Himalaya, the Western Ghats, the North–East India, and the Andaman & Nicobar Islands, are rich in unique species found nowhere else. Identifying and protecting these hotspots is a priority in conservation.

Ecosystem-Based Conservation: Different biomes (forests, wetlands, deserts, coasts, and mountains) support distinct life forms. Conservation strategies must suit the geographical setting; for example, mangrove protection along coasts or afforestation in mountains. Protected Areas: National parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, and World Heritage Sites are chosen based on geography to preserve critical habitats and prevent habitat fragmentation. Geographical Barriers and Corridors: Natural features like rivers, mountains, and valleys serve as barriers or corridors that influence animal movement and gene flow.

Conservation planning uses this knowledge to create wildlife corridors. Human–Environment Interaction: Geography also considers how local communities use land, water, and forests. Sustainable practices vary with geography, such as terrace farming in the hills or agroforestry in the plains. In short, biodiversity conservation is an intrinsic part of geography because the survival of species depends on their location, habitat conditions, and human activity within those regions.

Challenges Faced by People Living in Forests People living in forests often struggle to access essential facilities such as healthcare, education, and clean water. Women are exposed to fuelwood fumes and face, many health issues, making their daily lives difficult.

Forest dwellers depend heavily on forest produce such as firewood, honey, bamboo, and medicinal plants for their livelihood. Restrictions on forest use, deforestation, and the commercial exploitation of resources often limit their access to these resources. This creates a conflict between conservation laws and their survival needs, leading to economic insecurity. Forested hilly regions are prone to natural disasters such as floods and landslides. Floods can wash away homes, crops, and roads, while landslides can bury villages and cut off access to essential services.

Forest fires can quickly spread through dense vegetation, destroying homes and resources. Human care and preventive measures can help prevent many forest fires. Crops are often damaged by elephants, monkeys, or wild boars, and sometimes people face direct attacks. Such conflicts not only cause economic losses but also create fear and insecurity among forest communities. Many forest dwellers also face discrimination and neglect from mainstream society. They are often engaged in selling forest products at relatively low prices. Therefore, creating opportunities for processing and marketing these products is essential to enhance their income.

Forest communities also require assistance in accessing government schemes and programmes, as well as greater awareness of their legal rights. 2 – Life on Earth Ecological Commons—Shared Resources The term ecological commons refer to natural resources like forests, rivers, lakes, grazing lands, air, and biodiversity that are shared by a community and used collectively for its survival and well-being. Unlike private property, these resources are not owned by any single individual but belong to the community as a whole, and are often managed through traditional rules and practices. For centuries, people have depended on the ecological commons for food, water, fuel, fodder, and medicinal plants.

However, with population growth, industrial use, and privatisation, many of these commons are shrinking or degrading. Protecting ecological commons is important not only for the livelihoods of rural and tribal communities but also for maintaining ecological balance, regulating climate, and conserving biodiversity. The Big Questions Chapter 3 The period between 1000 CE and 1700 CE witnessed profound political, social, and cultural changes. The Indian subcontinent experienced repeated invasions and wars accompanied by religious discrimination and social distress.

Regional powers frequently resisted invaders who were making inroads into their territories. This resistance took both military and cultural forms. Nonetheless, this period manifested the resilience of the Indian civilisation, which safeguarded its core ideas and values. Indian society not only defended itself from external threats but also preserved its traditions. In this chapter, we will see how resistance and resilience shaped this period of Indian history. Let us begin by understanding the meaning of resistance and resilience in the context of the period under study and how they are interconnected.

Resilience refers to the capacity to, survive and adapt in challenging situations, including times of political unrest and instability. It is also about how communities and groups across diverse regions respond to challenges and opportunities. This capacity to absorb and adapt to hardship while preserving inherited socio-cultural and spiritual traditions can also be understood as resilience. The idea of India's resilient spirit extends beyond political and military spheres.

Resistance means actively opposing or challenging a force, authority, or threat in order to protect political power, territory, interests, or cultural and spiritual identity.

Resistance may take the form of warfare, alliances, diplomacy, negotiation, or other political actions. Resistance and resilience are, in fact, closely linked. Resilience is the backbone of resistance. While a political cause or leadership provides the condition for resistance, the ability to endure comes from resilience. Together, resistance and resilience help explain how Indian society sustained itself through different ages, particularly the period under study. This period is characterised by both conflict and cooperation, rather than being merely a story of invasion and resistance.

Safeguarding Sovereignty: Resistance, Alliances, and Confederacies From the 7th century onwards, the Indian subcontinent witnessed successive phases of invasions driven by territorial expansion and religious motives. It may also be noted that the surplus agrarian produce of the fertile plains fed by perennial river systems contributed to the people's economic well-being and also became a major reason for the invasions. The new state introduced administrative practices that led to greater centralisation of authority. For example, the iqta system, under which territories were assigned to military commanders in lieu of salaries, became a mechanism for land revenue collection and a system that increased the burden on the peasantry. Furthermore, during their military campaigns for territorial expansion, the forces of the Sultanate demolished sites sacred to the local communities. This led to stiff resistance from several kingdoms and chieftains.

Therefore, resistance throughout the Delhi Sultanate was fuelled by both political factors and the determination to preserve socio-cultural continuity. For instance, the Yādava dynasty of western Deccan (Devagiri), several Rajput dynasties of present-day Rajasthan, the Kākatīya rulers of eastern Deccan (Warangal), and the Hoysālas of present-day Karnataka repeatedly resisted the Sultans of Delhi. These states played an important role in checking the expansion of the Sultanate.

Over the years and under different Sultans, the Delhi Sultanate faced opposition and defiance from several states and regions including Mewar, Gwalior, Malwa, Awadh, Etawah, Ajmer, Jalore, Kalinjar, and Kannauj.

First, Zahiruddin Muhammad, also known as Bābur, from Central Asia launched an invasion on India. Second, Indian rulers began to assert their own authority.

In 1526, Bābur defeated the Lodi forces in the First Battle of Panipat, bringing the Sultanate to an end. In 1527, Rāṇā Sangrām Singh I, popularly known as Rāṇā Sāngā, of Mewar led a Rajput confederacy against Bābur in the Battle of Khanua. The battle ended in favour of Bābur and is seen as an important turning point in Indian history. As Mughal rule consolidated its power, relations between the Rajputs and the Mughals evolved over time, shaped by strategic considerations. Some Rajput kingdoms such as Mewar, maintained stiff resistance to Mughal authority, while others like the Kachhwāha Rajputs of Amber, negotiated cooperative relationships.

The Mughals, for their part, had a strong incentive to collaborate with the Rajputs—they needed the Rajputs' military might, their loyalty as well as their administrative strength to consolidate and stabilise the Mughal Empire. Towards this end, the Mughals integrated some of the Rajputs into the empire through the grant of mansabs and other understandings. The Ahom Kingdom: Centuries of Endurance The Ahom kingdom of Assam maintained its political independence for almost six centuries (1228–1826) and successfully resisted several invasions and attempts at annexation.

The military strategy of the Ahoms relied on exploiting the local terrain rather than engaging in direct confrontation. Ahom commanders possessed detailed knowledge of Assam's forests, river systems, and monsoon cycles, which invading forces generally lacked. Despite repeated attempts by the Mughals to annex the Brahmaputra valley, the Ahoms successfully defended their territories against Mughal invasion.

3 – Resistance and Resilience (1000–1700 CE) The first Ahom–Mughal clash took place in 1615 near Samdhara. Mughal forces under Abu Bakr made early gains but were soon compelled to retreat. By 1616, the Ahoms had recovered the lost territory, setting a pattern that would recur over the next sixty years. In 1662, Mīr Jumlā captured the Ahom capital, Garhgaon. Subsequently, a treaty was imposed on King Jayadhvaj Singha. However, the king defied the Mughals and renounced the treaty within a year of the Mughal withdrawal, and the Ahoms retained their independence.

A decisive check on Mughal ambitions in the region came in 1671, when the Ahom commander Lachit Borphukan defeated a Mughal fleet at the Battle of Saraighat, securing the Brahmaputra as an effective territorial boundary. The Ahoms' successful resistance against the might of the Mughal empire is a remarkable story of bravery, pride, and endurance. Ahom endurance rested on a combination of strategic alliance-building, guerrilla tactics, Assam's challenging geography, and the Paik system (about which you have read in Grade 8) of military-administrative organisation.

The Ahom navy also played a key role, using light, fast boats, called bāchārī, built specifically for river warfare, which gave them an advantage over Mughal fleets. Fig. 3.7. A monument at Guwahati, Assam commemorating the Battle of Saraighat Fig. 3.8. Model of a bāchārī boat

Understanding Society: India and Beyond Grade 9 Part 2 Vijayanagara Empire: Resilience against Expansion Resistance to foreign invasions was not confined to northern India. In the Deccan and beyond, the expanding campaigns of the Delhi Sultanate steadily weakened the older kingdoms of the south. Malik Kāfūr, Alauddin Khiljī's general, attacked major cities and temples, including those at Warangal, Belur, and Madurai.

Later, Muhammad bin Tughlaq's rise to power extended the Sultanate's influence even farther south, ultimately contributing to the decline of the Pandya Kingdom and the eventual emergence of a new sultanate territory known as the Madurai Sultanate. It was against this backdrop that the Vijayanagara Empire rose in 1336 to check the expansion of the Sultanate into peninsular India. Harihara and Bukkā established the independent kingdom of Vijayanagara—meaning 'City of Victory'—located near present-day Hampi, Karnataka.

The region's geography, including a formidable river and rugged, rocky terrain, provided Vijayanagara with a strong natural defence and a secure base for military operations. They made determined efforts to defend and expand their state's frontiers. The empire gradually expanded by annexing territory south of the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers and became one of the richest and most influential states, encouraging the flourishing of literature in Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, and Sanskrit. Vijayanagara's capital city became a centre of trade, culture, and political power in southern India.

During Bukkā's reign, Vijayanagara made major territorial gains, including the subjugation of the Madurai Sultanate and the annexation of Arcot. In 1342, the ageing Hoysāla king Vīra Ballāla III Fig. 3.9. An aerial view of Hampi, the capital of the Vijayanagara Empire

Understanding Society: India and Beyond Grade 9 Part 2 Due to the growing socio-cultural influence of the Sikh Gurus, the Mughal state increasingly intervened in their affairs from the beginning of the 17th century. As the Guru's influence was increasing, Jahāngīr ordered the execution of Guru Arjan Dev (the fifth Sikh guru) on the pretext of the Guru's alleged support to Jahāngīr's rebellious son, Khusrau Mirza. The martyrdom of Guru Arjan Dev marked a significant turning point in the history of the Sikhs and contributed to a gradual shift in their organisational and political orientation.

Later, Guru Hargobind (the sixth Sikh Guru) was detained by Jahāngīr in Gwalior Fort. During this period, the Sikhs visited Gwalior in large numbers and paid their respects to the Guru from outside the fortress. In 1675, Aurangzeb ordered the execution of Guru Tegh Bahādur, the ninth Sikh Guru. The martyrdom proved a turning point in Indian history. The brutality of the Mughal state against the Sikh Gurus particularly Guru Arjan Dev, Guru Tegh Bahādur, and the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh has few comparisons in history. The valour and sacrifice of the Gurus for the cause of the faith became the defining features of Sikhism.

Beyond political motivations, the act was also deeply rooted in the rigid religious and discriminatory practices of the Mughals. The martyrdom of the Sikh Gurus to uphold their faith and principles firmed the conviction of the Sikhs that persecution had to be met with firm resistance and resilience. Such persecution and political pressure could only be countered through collective organisation, and armed resistance as and when required. Many armed conflicts took place between the Sikhs and the Mughals. Guru Hargobind established the Akāl Takht, a seat of temporal authority, to administer justice and address matters of governance.

Scholars suggest that the establishment of the Akāl Takht was intended, in part, to counter Mughal political dominance. The concept of mīrī-pīrī became vital in this context, representing the Guru's authority over both spiritual (pīrī) and worldly (mīrī) affairs. In Amritsar, the Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) represented spiritual authority (pīrī), while temporal power (mīrī) was represented by the Akāl Takht. Bhakti Tradition: Affirmation of the Spirit of Resilience India underwent a profound transformation in its religious and spiritual landscape between the 11th and 17th centuries. From the 7th century onwards, the rise and expansion of Bhakti in peninsular India shaped social, religious, and political life. Bhakti tradition emphasised inclusivity, socio-religious equality, simplicity, and connecting with people's everyday life. For instance, Eknāth composed in Marathi and propagated a devotional path that was accessible to all without dependence on institutions.

The Bhakti tradition not only provided a spiritual refuge, but also played a role in preserving and transmitting core cultural traditions.

3 – Resistance and Resilience (1000–1700 CE) Temples: The Resilience of Sacred Sites Temples functioned as central pillars of the region's socio-economic and political life. These religious institutions evolved into major economic hubs that managed extensive land grants, provided employment to hundreds of specialised workers, and served as financial institutions for local traders. Rulers used temple patronage to strengthen their political legitimacy.

Beyond their spiritual and religious functions, temples facilitated social integration and served as centres of education and culture, where artistic traditions such as Bharatanatyam and many other art forms were preserved. They also exercised quasi-judicial authority, collecting local taxes and administering legal penalties. Temples also served as sources of legitimacy for political authority. The deities of these temples were regarded as protectors of the state and its people. In some cases, the deity was regarded as the ruler, while the actual ruler governed as the deity's deputy.

For example, the Gajapati rulers of Odisha called themselves the Rauta (deputy) of Jagannath. Similarly, the Kachhwāhā rulers of Jaipur governed on behalf of Govindadevajī, while the Rajput rulers of Kota regarded themselves as representatives of Rāma. Temples in India also functioned as significant economic institutions. They provided employment to a wide range of groups, including architects, artisans, sculptors, priests, musicians, and administrative staff. As substantial landholders, temples received donations, endowments, and land grants, often given as acts of Fig. 3.22. Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple, Srirangam

3 – Resistance and Resilience (1000–1700 CE) The main source of state income was land revenue, and the expanding frontiers of empires resulted in an increase in the area under cultivation. Over time, the collection of land revenue became increasingly strict and exploitative at various levels of administration. For example, during the reigns of Alauddin Khiljī and Mohammad bin Tughlaq, the land tax was raised to as much as 50 per cent of total agricultural production, in addition to other taxes. Moreover, the Sultans of Delhi, and later the Mughals had limited role in maritime trade.

Their concerns regarding coastal areas and port cities were largely confined to political and military matters and, to some extent, the collection of customs duties. As a result, coastal areas and their commerce remained largely in the hands of regional power holders and local communities. Irrigation technologies such as rope pulleys, spinning wheel, and Persian wheel were widely used by local populations, resulting in enhanced agricultural and economic output. In the Vijayanagara Empire, agricultural production varied greatly in both form and scale.

Consequently, irrigation systems ranged from extensive canal networks to small rain-fed patches of land. A defining feature of the Vijayanagara economy was its investment in small-scale irrigation. In addition to agricultural expansion, the period witnessed significant growth in trade and commerce. India's inland regions were connected to trade routes in Central Asia, facilitating a substantial flow of goods and artisanal knowledge, much of it carried by large groups of traders known as caravans. Inland trade networks expanded alongside the growth of urban centres.

Local trading communities such as the banjārās, along with revenue- collecting officials, played a crucial role in connecting rural regions with urban centres. From the 13th century onwards, seaborne trade grew significantly, with trading networks linking western India to the Persian Gulf and the Arabian Sea. Gradually, India became a major centre of the Indian Ocean trading network, with the eastern Mediterranean and China forming its vital axes until the arrival of Europeans in the subcontinent.

3 – Resistance and Resilience (1000–1700 CE) The World of the Indian Ocean: Continuity and Change With the turn of the 16th century, two major developments occurred—the arrival of Europeans for trading ventures and the Mughal conquest of northern India. The Europeans, particularly the Portuguese, and the Mughals entered an already established economic system in which local institutions and networks played a crucial role. The Portuguese attempted to establish greater control over oceanic trade and commerce, while the Mughals sought to centralise control over the land revenue system.

European involvement, which began with the Portuguese and was later followed by the Dutch, English, Danes, and French, developed into a complex system of interactions between European trading companies and Indian merchant networks. Subsequently, the Indian subcontinent became a major global intersection of commerce and cross-cultural exchange. Simultaneously, new merchant groups emerged in coastal and hinterland areas. They controlled wealth, production system, supply chains, and at the same time, funded states and supported their political allies.

The peasantry was involved in the production of raw materials, while weavers, dyers, bleachers, and other groups were working regularly to ready the deliveries of cotton textiles. Before the 15th century, the Indian Ocean trading network had a huge presence of Arab, Chinese, and Indian merchants. In subsequent centuries, Gujarati merchants in particular emerged as significant Fig. 3.31. A painting of a woman weaver

Alongside them, numerous merchant groups flourished in Malabar, Coromandel, and Bengal, adapting to the growing influence and competition of the British, Dutch, and French. These merchant groups were not merely involved in the buying and selling of goods, but were closely connected to the political economy, facilitating and financing trade. Indian merchants functioned as traders, shippers, bankers, money-changers, brokers, dubhaśhīs (interpreters and translators), diplomats, and bureaucrats.

Mercantile activities were not limited to a few, select communities. For instance, vellalār, who were traditionally agriculturists and pastoralists, participated in the Indian Ocean trading network in various capacities. From the 16th century onwards, many peasant groups began to participate actively in commerce. Some of them even learnt new languages, including Portuguese, French, English, and Persian, to facilitate their commercial activities.

4 – Governance and Public Policy Solving public problems requires much more than a government issuing orders. Different institutions and citizens need to work together, make decisions, implement them effectively, and remain accountable. This process is known as governance.

Understanding Government and Governance Government Governance Refers to the institutions that exercise political authority Refers to the process of decision-making and implementation Includes the Legislature, the Executive, and the Judiciary Includes government, citizens, media, civil society, and private organisations Focuses on who governs Focuses on how governing is carried out The terms 'government' and 'governance' are closely related. However, they are not synonymous.

Government refers to the institutions and authorities that exercise political power, while governance refers to the process by which decisions are made, implemented, and monitored in the public interest. The government formulates and implements people-centric policies, and good governance ensures that these policies are transparent, accountable, effective, and responsive to people's needs. Governance is the system through which decisions are made, implemented, and monitored for the welfare of the people. It refers to the way a country, state, city, village, school, or organisation is managed.

Evolution of Governance in India In the previous section, we studied that while the government is the institutional aspect, governance refers to its functional aspect.

The government's institutional setup influences the nature of governance, and governance initiatives, in turn, require institutional adaptations to implement policies and schemes. We are familiar with the structure of government at different levels in India. But the same structure has not always existed as it does now; it has evolved from certain historical experiences. Let us understand this historical context by looking at the 'big picture' of the world history. Do you remember the phenomenon of colonialism that you learnt about in Grade 8?

We know that European powers colonised many societies, particularly those in Asia, Africa, and the Americas. Before colonial rulers forced their own models of governance and policy-making on colonised people, these societies governed themselves in accordance with local and organic systems. Although most colonies had become independent by the end of the 20th century, colonial institutions largely persisted, and their structures continued to dominate even in contemporary times. India is not an exception to the historical legacy of colonialism. However, India stands out in two important ways.

Firstly, unlike many societies that experienced colonial rule, India has preserved most of its knowledge of its pre-colonial institutions and traditions of governance through texts and practices. Secondly, after Independence in 1947, it was not possible to replace all colonial institutions at once. The leaders of independent India therefore framed the Constitution in the spirit of India's own values and ideals. Since Independence, Indian institutions have continued to draw upon traditional ideas and values of governance and have adapted them to the needs of a modern democracy.

The Making of a Public Policy A public policy is developed through a systematic process rather than a single decision. It usually begins when citizens, government officials, researchers, or civil society organisations realise that a new need has to be met, an existing problem has to be resolved, or a facility has to be made better in the interest of the people.

Then the government studies the issue, collects information, and consults experts, stakeholders, and the public to understand different viewpoints and possible solutions. Based on these discussions, the government authorities prepare, review, and approve a draft policy. Once the policy is approved by the concerned authorities, it is translated into programmes and schemes, which provide a clear framework for different ministries, departments, and local governments to take specific action. The implementation of any policy is continuously monitored and evaluated to assess whether it is achieving its objectives.

Feedback from citizens and other stakeholders is used to improve the policy over time. Thus, public policy is a continuous cycle of problem identification, consultation, policy formulation, implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and improvement. This process helps the government respond effectively to the changing needs of society.

6 – From Ideas to Startups India's Traditional Entrepreneurial Community Entrepreneurship in India has deep roots among traditional communities, where skills, occupations, and occupational knowledge have been passed down through generations. Long before modern startups, these communities practised self-employment, innovation, and trade, forming the backbone of India's local economy. The Chettiar (Nattukottai Chettiar) community from Tamil Nadu is a well-known traditional entrepreneurial community.

Historically, Chettiars were traders, bankers, and moneylenders, operating not only across India but also in Sri Lanka, Burma (now Myanmar), Malaysia, and other parts of Southeast Asia. They were known for:  Strong business ethics and trust-based lending  Excellent accounting and record-keeping skills  Reinvesting profits into trade, temples, education, and community welfare The Chettiar community built wealth through trade in salt, rice, textiles, and finance, often without formal banks.

Even today, Chettiar entrepreneurship inspires modern India by showing how risk-taking, discipline, and long-term vision can build sustainable businesses rooted in tradition. Fig. 6.12. Understanding Society: India and Beyond Grade 9 Part 2 Startups and Their Contribution to the Nation India's vibrant startup ecosystem is built not only on innovation but also on perseverance. All entrepreneurs should be aware that there is a chance of their business ending in failure. So while some startups grow rapidly, others struggle or even close down. As with other things in life, there is nothing wrong with failure if an honest effort has been made.

Hence, these experiences contribute to entrepreneurial learning, and every unsuccessful attempt offers lessons that help entrepreneurs develop stronger ideas and build better businesses in the future. As was famously said by Swami Vivekananda: With consistent hard work and perseverance, today, India is the third- largest startup ecosystem in the world, powered by its young and talented population.

The startup world is growing fast, driven by creativity and technological support, with around 120 unicorns (startups valued at over 1 billion dollars) in 2025. These are working in exciting fields, like e-commerce (online shopping), fin-tech (digital payments), health-tech (online healthcare), and agri-tech (farming technology). Cities like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Mumbai, and Delhi NCR have become major startup hubs. These ventures are creating jobs, supporting sustainability, and driving economic growth.

In recognition of the importance of promoting entrepreneurship, the government has introduced many schemes, such as Startup India, which supports the vision of Atmanirbhar Bharat, focusing on making India self-reliant through innovation and local solutions. As India moves towards the vision of Viksit Bharat 2047, entrepreneurship will continue to play a vital role in creating employment, driving innovation, empowering communities, and building a more prosperous, self-reliant, and sustainable nation.

The next generation of entrepreneurs may well be sitting in your classroom today, ready to transform ideas into solutions that make a meaningful difference to society.
